Q: How can I find the number of occurrences of a string in a file using the Windows command line? A:

The following script worked for me (the source file contained quote characters, and this is why I used the 'usebackq' parameter).

The caret sign(^) acts as the escape character in the Windows batch scripting language.

@setlocal enableextensions enabledelayedexpansion
SET TOTAL=0
FOR /F "usebackq tokens=*" %%I IN (file.txt) do (
    SET LN=%%I
    FOR %%J IN ("!LN!") do (
        FOR /F %%K IN ('ECHO %%J ^| FIND /I /C "searchPhrase"') DO (
            @SET /A TOTAL=!TOTAL!+%%K
        )
    )
)
ECHO Number of occurrences is !TOTAL!

Q: Count the number of occurrences of a string using sed A:

Never say never. Pure sed (although it may require the GNU version).

#!/bin/sed -nf
# Based on a script from the sed info file (info sed)
# section 4.8 Numbering Non-blank Lines (cat -b)
# modified to count lines that begin with "title"

/^title/! be

x
/^$/ s/^.*$/0/
/^9*$/ s/^/0/
s/.9*$/x&/
h
s/^.*x//
y/0123456789/1234567890/
x
s/x.*$//
G
s/\n//
h

:e

$ {x;p}

Explanation:

#!/bin/sed -nf
# Run sed without printing output by default (-n)
# using the following file as the sed script (-f)

/^title/! be        # If the current line doesn't begin with "title"
                    # branch to label e

x                   # Swap the counter from hold space into pattern space
/^$/ s/^.*$/0/      # If pattern space is empty start the counter at zero
/^9*$/ s/^/0/       # If pattern space starts with a nine, prepend a zero
s/.9*$/x&/          # Mark the position of the last digit
                    # before a sequence of nines (if any)
h                   # Copy the marked counter to hold space
s/^.*x//            # Delete everything before the marker
y/0123456789/1234567890/   # Increment the digits that were after the mark
x                   # Swap pattern space and hold space
s/x.*$//            # Delete everything after the marker leaving
                    # the leading digits
G                   # Append hold space to pattern space
s/\n//              # Remove the newline, leaving all the digits concatenated
h                   # Save the counter into hold space

:e                  # Label e

$ {x;p}             # If this is the last line of input,
                    # swap in the counter and print it

Q: Python bit for bitcoin transactions send() method doesn't work A:

As noted previously in November, the bit library's broadcast mechanism is fundamentally unreliable and outdated. This forces many developers to resort to manual broadcasting for successful Testnet transactions. However, after conducting an in-depth investigation into the root causes, I've identified exactly why this happens and provided a complete fix.

The broadcast failure stems from a cascading architectural failure that affects both Mainnet and Testnet environments not just a simple API misconfiguration.

The Deprecated Service Dependency Crisis ("Bit Rot")

The critical insight is that the bit library's NetworkAPI layer relies on a hardcoded dispatcher list of third-party blockchain APIs. This list has deteriorated significantly due to the library's age:

Smartbit ❌ Permanently Shut Down

Bitcore ❌ Unreliable/Unreachable

Blockchair ❌ Requires API Key

Blockstream ⚠️ Only viable provider, but with critical payload bug (see below)

This is what happens under the hood when you call .send():

# bit/network/services.py - NetworkAPI dispatcher

BROADCAST_TX_MAIN = [

BlockchairAPI.broadcast_tx, # ❌ Requires API key - fails silently

BlockstreamAPI.broadcast_tx,# ⚠️ Has payload formattingbug

BitcoreAPI.broadcast_tx, # ❌ Endpoints unreachable

SmartbitAPI.broadcast_tx, # ❌ Service shut down

BlockchainAPI.broadcast_tx, # ❌ No longer maintained]

BROADCAST_TX_TEST = [

BlockchairAPI.broadcast_tx_testnet, # ❌ Requires API key BlockstreamAPI.broadcast_tx_testnet,# ⚠️ Payloadbug

BitcoreAPI.broadcast_tx_testnet, # ❌ Unreachable

SmartbitAPI.broadcast_tx_testnet,# ❌ Shut down]

The dispatcher iterates through this list using round-robin logic. Most providers fail immediately (dead services), and the only remaining viable option Blockstream contains a critical protocol mismatch bug (see below). The library interprets these failures as transient network issues and cycles through the dead providers, eventually timing out or returning a silent failure.

The Compounding Issue: The Blockstream Payload Bug

Even when the dispatcher reaches Blockstream (the only operational provider), the request fails due to a malformed HTTP payload:

# BROKEN: The library wraps the hex in a dictionary

data = {cls.TX_PUSH_PARAM: tx_hex} # Sends: {'data': '01000...'}

r = requests.post(cls.MAIN_TX_PUSH_API, data=data, timeout=DEFAULT_TIMEOUT)

Blockstream's /tx endpoint expects the raw transaction hex as the request body, not as a form-encoded dictionary parameter. The server responds with a 400 Bad Request, which the dispatcher interprets as a service failure and cycles back to the defunct providers.

Result: The transaction is successfully signed (cryptographically valid), but never reaches the network mempool. Manual broadcasting via external tools (cURL, web explorers) works perfectly with the exact same transaction hex, confirming the fault lies entirely within the library's networking logic.

The Deep Dive Investigation

To isolate the problem, I decomposed the .send() operation into its atomic stages:

Stage 1: Signing (create_transaction) ✅ Functional

  • The method produces a valid, cryptographically correct raw hex string

  • Evidence: Manually broadcasting this hex via external tools succeeds

Stage 2: Broadcasting (NetworkAPI.broadcast_tx) ❌ Failed

  • The library's internal logic rejects the same hex that works externally

  • This pinpoints the failure to the NetworkAPI layer exclusively

By testing each endpoint independently with the signed transaction, I confirmed:

  • Blockstream accepts the raw hex directly via cURL: ✅ Success

  • Blockstream rejects the library's wrapped payload: ❌ Fails

  • All other providers are offline: ❌ Unreachable

This surgical diagnosis revealed the two-pronged root cause: outdated service dependencies compounded by a protocol mismatch in the only working provider.

The Complete Solution

I've published a corrected version at github.com/salimbk016/bit-broadcast-fix with full patch files and diagnostic documentation.

Q: Performance implications of compact representations A:

The answer as always is "it depends". In this case it really depends on the architecture you are targeting and the kind of operations you are doing on these structures.

Since I don't know your target architecture, I can give you some general considerations for x86 like architectures.

Compacting your data in the struct brings better cache locality when used in an array.

Encoding multiple variables in one field can mean a slower read/write access.

Aligning your data brings faster access.

By sorting your fields from biggest to smallest (when they are aligned) can reduce the struct size because of the alignment requirements.

If you want to know exactly how your code performs, I am afraid you need to actually run it and benchmark it on the actual architecture.

Q: Unable to install specific R packages A:

This problem also occurs on some Linux systems, where it can be solved in the following way (on Windows it might be similar, but I can't test this myself): The problem is with the package "units". When trying to install this package on Linux systems, a warning message states that the Linux package libudunits2-dev (for Ubuntu/Debian) is missing. Installing this by calling

sudo apt install libudunits2-dev

from the command line solves the problem. Afterwards sf can be installed as usual using

install.packages("sf)

Q: Azure Data Factory throwing "Invoking Azure function failed with HttpStatusCode - InternalServerError." A:

Call to provided Azure function 'OnCopySuccess' failed with status-'InternalServerError' and message - 'Invoking Azure function failed with HttpStatusCode - InternalServerError.

Has nothing to do with Azure DataFactory, it fails because of the Azure Functions, HAs from the error you will not be able to detect any issues so, you may examine the output of your azure function app using logs in kudu, in addition to the monitor of the azure function.

In addition, kudu log files are more timely than the Azure function's monitor. Simply navigate to this website's address. Click on the URL https://yourfunctionappname.scm.azurewebsites.net/DebugConsole

Go To: LogFiles\Application\Functions\Function\yourtriggername

The log files can then be found. The log file in Kudu is real-time, whereas the monitor takes a while to show (typically 5 minutes).

HTTP Function is supposed to actually return an HTTP result, See the Original Post - So you might check your Azure Function Code.
